title: German A1 | Interactive Grammar Lab
based_on: Independent CEFR A1 grammar curriculum. Maintains the step sequence of the user-provided grammar study material.

lessons.title: People, names and first verbs
lessons.goal: Introduce yourself and recognize informal/polite forms.
explanations: Use ich, du and Sie with the correct verb form. A German present-tense verb changes with the subject.
With ich use -e for many verbs; du often uses -st; polite Sie uses -en. The verb sein is irregular.

trap.why: Do not combine bin with an ordinary present-tense verb.

lessons.challenge: Say four true sentences: your name, country, town and language. Then change two sentences to du/Sie questions.
deep_notes: Meaning comes first: ask who is speaking before choosing the ending.
ich heiße, du heißt, Sie heißen: forms belong to different people.
Use the fixed polite pair Guten Tag! / Auf Wiedersehen! only in appropriate contexts.
The form Sie is written with a capital S when it means polite you.

quiz.explanation: Polite Sie uses the infinitive-shaped plural form.
Das takes the third-person singular ist.
The idiomatic question for someone's name starts with Wie.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Ich bin lerne Deutsch.
review_tasks.why: Do not combine bin with an ordinary present-tense verb.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: ich + verb + information
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Du kommst aus Portugal.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Sind Sie Frau Richter?
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: W-questions and verb position
lessons.goal: Ask where, who, what and how, and build correct statements.
explanations: For a W-question, put the question word first and the conjugated verb immediately after it.
In statements the conjugated verb takes position two; position one may be a whole phrase, not just one word.

examples.en: How does one write your name?

trap.why: In a direct W-question, the finite verb follows the question word.

lessons.challenge: Ask a partner their name, home town and native language. Say one answer starting with a place.
deep_notes: Question words carry meaning: wer for people, wo for a location, woher for origin, wann for time.
Compare Wo wohnst du? (location) with Woher kommst du? (origin).
Even long first elements count as ONE slot before a conjugated verb.
The form of the verb still matches its subject after inversion.

fill_questions.explanation: After the initial place, the verb comes second.

quiz.explanation: The verb comes second after the place.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Wo du wohnst?
review_tasks.why: In a direct W-question, the finite verb follows the question word.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: W-word + verb + person + rest?
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Wie schreibt man deinen Namen?
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: In Augsburg wohnt mein Freund.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Present tense, haben and nicht
lessons.goal: Use all six persons and negate statements accurately.
lessons.formula: subject + finite verb + nicht + relevant information
explanations: Common endings: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. After stems ending -t or -d, du and er forms often need an extra -e-.
Use haben for possession and nicht for negating verbs, adjectives or phrases. Position of nicht depends on what is negated.

examples.en: She does not live in Bonn.

trap.why: arbeiten requires arbeitet with ihr.

lessons.challenge: Describe your class with wir and ihr; add two negative statements about today.
deep_notes: Verb endings follow person, not the number of people physically present in a scene.
Learn sein and haben separately: bin/bist/ist and habe/hast/hat.
Negating an adjective differs from negating an unspecified noun: nicht teuer but kein Geld.
Introduce a number by reading it, then saying it within a full sentence.

quiz.explanation: The ihr form of sein is seid.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Ihr arbeitst am Samstag.
review_tasks.why: arbeiten requires arbeitet with ihr.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: subject + finite verb + nicht + relevant information
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Ihr habt heute Unterricht.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Sie wohnt nicht in Bonn.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Yes/no questions and possession
lessons.goal: Ask yes/no questions and answer negative questions with doch.
explanations: Move the conjugated verb to the first position in a yes/no question. Do not use English-style do.
Use doch to contradict a negative question. Use mein/meine and dein/deine with grammatical gender and number.

examples.de: Wohnst du nicht hier? Doch, ich wohne hier.
examples.en: Don't you live here? Yes, I do.

trap.why: For a neutral yes/no question, begin with the verb.

lessons.challenge: Make three yes/no questions, including one negative question that you answer with doch.
deep_notes: A simple statement becomes a neutral question when the finite verb moves first.
Ja confirms a positive question; nein rejects it; doch contradicts a negative proposition.
Possessive article endings follow grammatical gender, not who owns the object.
If unsure how to answer, repeat the verb in a complete sentence.

quiz.explanation: Begin yes/no questions with the finite verb.

quiz.prompt: Du wohnst nicht hier? ___, ich wohne hier!

quiz.explanation: Ask about a state with Ist sie ...?

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Du hast Geschwister?
review_tasks.why: For a neutral yes/no question, begin with the verb.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: finite verb + subject + rest?
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Wohnst du nicht hier? Doch, ich wohne hier.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Das ist meine Schwester.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Noun gender and pronouns
lessons.goal: Use der, das, die and the matching subject pronouns.
explanations: Every German noun has grammatical gender. Learn the noun with its article, not alone.
Replace a named object by er (der), es (das) or sie (die); all plural nouns use sie.

examples.de: Der Rucksack ist schwer. Er ist voll.
examples.en: The backpack is heavy. It is full.

examples.de: Das Fenster ist offen. Es ist groß.
examples.en: The window is open. It is large.

examples.de: Die Brille ist neu. Sie ist schön.
examples.en: The glasses are new. They are nice.

trap.wrong: Das Auto ist alt. Er ist kaputt.
trap.correct: Das Auto ist alt. Es ist kaputt.
trap.why: Auto is neuter: das -> es.

lessons.challenge: Look around you. Name six objects with articles; replace each with the right pronoun.
deep_notes: Article and pronoun are a pair: der/er; das/es; die/sie.
Plural nouns all use die as definite article, regardless of singular gender.
The noun's gender is a grammar feature: do not infer it from an object's natural sex.
Adjectives after sein usually have no gender ending: Der Stuhl ist klein.

fill_questions.prompt: Der Fernseher ist groß. ___ ist modern.
Das Zimmer ist klein. ___ ist hell.

quiz.prompt: Das Fahrrad ist neu. ___ ist schnell.
Der Baum ist alt. ___ ist hoch.
Die Uhr ist kaputt. ___ geht nicht.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Das Auto ist alt. Er ist kaputt.
review_tasks.model: Das Auto ist alt. Es ist kaputt.
review_tasks.why: Auto is neuter: das -> es.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: article + noun -> er / es / sie
review_tasks.model: Der Rucksack ist schwer. Er ist voll.
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Das Fenster ist offen. Es ist groß.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Die Brille ist neu. Sie ist schön.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: ein, eine, kein and nicht
lessons.goal: Distinguish an indefinite noun from a negated noun or adjective.
explanations: Use ein for masculine and neuter nominative nouns; eine for feminine nouns. Kein follows similar endings and can negate plural nouns.
Use nicht for adjective, verb and specific-phrase negation: nicht teuer, nicht hier, nicht der Schlüssel.

trap.why: Negating an indefinite count noun normally requires kein.

lessons.challenge: Describe five household items, including two things you do not have.
deep_notes: First mention an object with ein/eine; refer to the specific known object with der/die/das.
Kein replaces ein or negates a noun without an article, including a plural noun.
Nicht denies properties, verbs, locations and specific noun phrases.
In the accusative case some ein/kein forms change; see Step 7.

quiz.explanation: A specific possessive phrase is negated with nicht.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Das ist nicht Computer.
review_tasks.why: Negating an indefinite count noun normally requires kein.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: Das ist + ein/eine/kein/keine + noun
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Wir haben keine Milch.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Der Laptop ist nicht teuer.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Plurals and accusative
lessons.goal: Use plural nouns and change masculine objects into den/einen.
explanations: Learn plural forms with each noun; endings can be -e, -en, -er, -s or zero.
In the accusative, masculine articles change: der->den, ein->einen, kein->keinen. Feminine and neuter articles generally stay the same.

trap.why: A masculine accusative object needs einen.

lessons.challenge: Write a shopping list with six nouns and say three full sentences about what you need.
deep_notes: Ask who performs the action (nominative) and what receives it (accusative).
Only masculine singular definite/indefinite articles visibly change in this simple case comparison.
Many feminine nouns make plural with -(e)n, but don't rely on guesses for every noun.
Keep a vocabulary record: article + singular + plural + a model sentence.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Ich sehe ein Mann.
review_tasks.why: A masculine accusative object needs einen.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: subject + verb + einen/den + masculine object
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Wir kaufen die Bücher.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Kennst du den Lehrer?
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: können and sentence bracket
lessons.goal: Say what you can do and keep the second verb at the end.
explanations: Modal verbs such as können occupy the conjugated verb position; the full verb appears as infinitive at the end.
Some strong verbs change vowels with du and er/sie/es (fahren->fährst, lesen->liest).

examples.en: I can cook in the evening.

examples.de: Mein Bruder fährt jeden Tag Rad.

trap.why: After a modal, use the infinitive at the end.

lessons.challenge: Say three things you can do, two things you cannot do and one question to a classmate.
deep_notes: A conjugated modal and a final infinitive form a sentence bracket.
If you start with time, the modal still stays second: Heute kann ich kommen.
Strong vowel change is limited to some verbs and mostly du and er/sie/es.
Compare können (ability) with dürfen (permission), learned later.

quiz.explanation: After kann, use infinitive at sentence end.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Sie kann spricht Deutsch.
review_tasks.why: After a modal, use the infinitive at the end.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: subject + können + details + infinitive
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Kannst du gut schwimmen?
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Mein Bruder fährt jeden Tag Rad.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Time phrases and word order
lessons.goal: Begin sentences with time and say when events happen.
lessons.formula: time phrase + finite verb + subject + rest
explanations: When a time expression begins a statement, the conjugated verb still comes second: Morgen komme ich.
Use am for days and parts of days; um for clock times. halb acht = 7:30.

examples.de: Um halb acht beginnt mein Kurs.
examples.en: My class starts at half past seven.

trap.why: Time is first; the conjugated verb must remain second.

lessons.challenge: Explain your schedule for three days and give precise times.
deep_notes: German's halb refers to the coming hour: halb vier is 3:30.
Use um with a specific clock time, not with a weekday.
A time phrase at the start pushes the subject behind the finite verb.
For dates and months use different expressions; don't treat all time words alike.

quiz.explanation: halb neun means half toward nine.
The verb takes the second position.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Morgen ich arbeite.
review_tasks.why: Time is first; the conjugated verb must remain second.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: time phrase + finite verb + subject + rest
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Um halb acht beginnt mein Kurs.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Heute Abend komme ich später.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: mögen, möchte and ordering
lessons.goal: Express likes, polite wishes and food choices.
explanations: mögen describes preference; möchte is a polite wish or request. Essen and nehmen have irregular du/er forms.
The food or drink is commonly a direct object, so masculine nouns often need einen or den.

examples.en: I'd like an apple juice, please.

examples.de: Was nimmst du? Ich nehme einen Salat.
examples.en: What will you have? I'll take a salad.

trap.why: Kaffee is masculine and an accusative object.

lessons.challenge: Order three things politely, then explain one thing you do not like.
deep_notes: Use mögen for lasting tastes; möchte is useful for a polite request now.
Memorize the natural chunk Ich hätte gern later; for now Ich möchte is enough.
Masculine direct objects often require einen, even for drinks.
Compound nouns inherit gender from the final noun: der Saft -> der Orangensaft.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Ich möchte ein Kaffee.
review_tasks.why: Kaffee is masculine and an accusative object.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: ich möchte + accusative object + bitte
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Ich möchte einen Apfelsaft, bitte.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Was nimmst du? Ich nehme einen Salat.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Separable verbs
lessons.goal: Build sentences with separable verb prefixes and recognize infinitives.
explanations: With separable verbs, the conjugated stem appears in position two and the prefix moves to the end of a main clause.
With a modal verb the entire infinitive stays together at the end: Ich muss früh aufstehen.

examples.de: Um sieben Uhr stehe ich auf.
Der Bus fährt um acht Uhr ab.

trap.correct: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.
trap.why: The prefix of aufstehen separates in this main clause.

lessons.challenge: Describe your morning with four separable verbs and one modal sentence.
deep_notes: The detachable prefix may move to the very end after objects and time phrases.
Modal + separable infinitive stays together: Ich kann jetzt aufstehen.
In a direct yes/no question the finite stem comes first and the prefix last.
Keep accents on the prefix when speaking (AUFstehen); it helps recognition.

fill_questions.explanation: The prefix an goes to the end.
The conjugated stem of ankommen is kommt.

quiz.explanation: aufstehen separates in a simple main clause.
abfahren separates in a main clause.
The prefix zu separates in present-tense main clauses.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Ich aufstehe um sechs Uhr.
review_tasks.model: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.
review_tasks.why: The prefix of aufstehen separates in this main clause.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: subject + conjugated verb + ... + prefix
review_tasks.model: Um sieben Uhr stehe ich auf.
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Der Bus fährt um acht Uhr ab.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Ich kann dich später anrufen.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Perfekt with haben
lessons.goal: Talk about completed actions with haben and a participle.
explanations: For many past events, use the present tense of haben plus the past participle at sentence end.
Regular participles often use ge-...-t; many irregular verbs use -en. Verbs ending -ieren form participles without ge-.

examples.en: Did you make a phone call today?

trap.why: A completed past action requires the participle.

lessons.challenge: Tell a partner what you did yesterday using at least five different participles.
deep_notes: Perfekt has two parts: auxiliary verb and past participle, separated in a main clause.
Some common irregular participles have vowel changes; learn them as vocabulary.
Separable verbs insert ge- after the prefix: aufgeräumt, angerufen.
-ieren verbs never add ge-: organisiert, repariert.

quiz.explanation: The participle of hören is gehört.
Anrufen uses haben with du hast.
Verbs in -ieren form participles without ge-.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Ich habe gestern einkaufen.
review_tasks.why: A completed past action requires the participle.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: subject + haben + time/object + Partizip II
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Wir haben einen Film gesehen.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Hast du heute telefoniert?
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Perfekt with sein and past states
lessons.goal: Choose sein for many movement/change verbs and use war/hatte.
explanations: Many intransitive movement and change-of-state verbs form Perfekt with sein; bleiben also uses sein.
For sein and haben themselves, everyday German often uses war and hatte for the past.

trap.why: gehen forms Perfekt with sein.

lessons.challenge: Tell a short story: where you went, what you did and how the day was.
deep_notes: Compare an action (ich bin gefahren) with a past state (ich war müde).
Not every verb about movement takes sein in every context; learn common A1 patterns first.
The participle still goes last when sein is the auxiliary.
Since the event may involve several verbs, choose auxiliary for each separately.

fill_questions.explanation: The past of sein for wir is waren.

quiz.explanation: The past of sein is war.
The past of haben is hatte.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Wir haben nach Hause gegangen.
review_tasks.why: gehen forms Perfekt with sein.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: subject + bin/ist/sind + ... + Partizip II
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Wir sind am Sonntag gewandert.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Letzte Woche hatte ich Urlaub.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: es gibt and dative pronouns
lessons.goal: Describe what exists and say what people like.
lessons.formula: es gibt + accusative; es gefällt + dative person
explanations: es gibt takes an accusative object even if the noun is plural.
Dative pronouns such as mir, dir, ihm, ihr express whom something pleases or to whom something is given.

examples.de: In der Stadt gibt es einen Park.
examples.en: There is a park in town.
How do you like the square?

trap.why: A plural subject requires gefallen.

lessons.challenge: Describe two places in your town, saying what exists and what you like.
deep_notes: es gibt can be used with singular or plural objects, but the verb remains gibt.
Ask Was gibt es hier? then answer with an accusative noun phrase.
gefallen has a different structure from mögen: Das Haus gefällt mir.
With plural nouns the finite verb gefallen is plural, not gefällt.

quiz.explanation: es gibt is a fixed singular expression.
helfen takes dative; uns is dative plural.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Mir gefällt die Cafés.
review_tasks.why: A plural subject requires gefallen.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: es gibt + accusative; es gefällt + dative person
review_tasks.model: In der Stadt gibt es einen Park.
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Das Museum gefällt mir.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Wie gefällt dir der Platz?
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Dative articles and location
lessons.goal: Use mit, zu, bei and wo? with dative articles.
explanations: Dative articles are dem (masculine/neuter), der (feminine), den (plural). Plural nouns often add -n if possible.
After mit, bei, zu, aus and von, use dative. For static location with in, also use dative.

trap.why: mit always requires dative.

lessons.challenge: Give directions to three places using mit, zu and in.
deep_notes: Learn dative as the usual partner of mit, zu, bei, aus, von, nach and seit.
Remember masculine/neuter dem, feminine der, plural den (often with noun -n).
Wo? can use in + dative for a fixed location.
Do not automatically use dative after every in: direction needs accusative (Step 24).

quiz.explanation: mit takes dative, Taxi is neuter.
aus takes dative, die Schweiz -> der Schweiz.
Static position in a feminine place -> der.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Ich fahre mit die Bahn.
review_tasks.why: mit always requires dative.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: mit + dem/der/den; in + dative location
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Sie wohnt bei ihrer Tante.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Wir sind in der Bibliothek.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Possessives in different cases
lessons.goal: Choose possessive endings for gender and grammatical case.
explanations: Possessive words take endings similar to ein. Their form depends on gender, number and case.
Nominative masculine: mein Bruder; accusative masculine: meinen Bruder; dative masculine: meinem Bruder.

trap.why: kennen takes an accusative object.

lessons.challenge: Describe family, friends and belongings in five original sentences using different possessives.
deep_notes: Possessives combine owner (mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser) with endings from gender and case.
Masculine accusative is easy to notice: mein Bruder -> meinen Bruder.
Dative masculine/neuter normally ends -em: meinem Vater, meinem Kind.
Plural and feminine forms look similar in some positions; always ask case and number.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Ich kenne mein Bruder.
review_tasks.why: kennen takes an accusative object.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: mein/dein/sein/ihr/unser + matching ending + noun
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.prompt: Change the person, place or time while keeping the grammar correct:
review_tasks.question: Ich besuche meinen Onkel.
review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Sie hilft ihrer Mutter.
review_tasks.why: Many answers are valid; check the grammar, not word-for-word similarity.

lessons.title: Time prepositions and polite requests
lessons.goal: Talk about time spans and ask politely with könnten.
explanations: Use in zwei Stunden for a future time, vor zwei Tagen for time ago, and nach der Arbeit for after work.
For polite requests, könnten + Sie/du ... + infinitive at end. Learn the whole phrase; it is less direct than an imperative.

examples.de: Vor einer Woche war ich krank.
examples.en: I was ill a week ago.

trap.wrong: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen machen?
trap.why: Only the infinitive helfen is required at the end.

lessons.challenge: Ask for help twice: one informal request and one polite request to an official.
deep_notes: in can point forward in time: in einer Stunde = one hour from now.
vor + dative time measures backward: vor zwei Tagen.
nach + dative marks a sequence: nach dem Mittagessen.
Könnten Sie ...? is a useful polite phrase; the second verb belongs at the end.

fill_questions.explanation: in einer Stunde = one hour from now.

quiz.explanation: in five minutes refers to future.

quiz.prompt: ___ dem Unterricht gehen wir nach Hause.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen machen?
review_tasks.why: Only the infinitive helfen is required at the end.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: in/vor/nach + time; Könnten Sie ... + infinitive?
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

lessons.title: wollen, werden, mit and ohne
lessons.goal: Express plans, change and accompaniment.
explanations: wollen expresses intention. werden can describe becoming something or changing state.
mit takes dative; ohne normally takes accusative. Contrast mit dem Bus and ohne einen Regenschirm.

examples.en: We want to travel in summer.
It gets dark in the evening.

trap.why: The modal structure keeps its infinitives at the end.

lessons.challenge: State three plans, one change in the weather and one journey with/without something.
deep_notes: wollen is about intention, not the only way to speak about future plans.
werden as a main verb means become; don't use it for every future plan at A1.
mit takes dative (mit meinem Freund); ohne takes accusative (ohne meinen Freund).
Modal forms are irregular: ich will, du willst, er will.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:

review_tasks.why: The modal structure keeps its infinitives at the end.

lessons.title: Polite commands and sollen
lessons.goal: Give formal instructions and relay advice or obligations.
explanations: The polite imperative uses the infinitive plus Sie: Kommen Sie bitte herein!
sollen expresses advice/instructions from another person; the main verb remains in the infinitive at the end.

examples.de: Ich soll morgen zum Arzt gehen.
examples.en: I'm supposed to go to the doctor tomorrow.

trap.why: The polite command uses the infinitive Warten followed by Sie.

lessons.challenge: Write three courteous signs for a classroom, office or waiting room.
deep_notes: Polite imperative: infinitive first, then Sie. Adding bitte makes it friendlier.
Do not confuse a polite command with a declarative sentence ending in Sie.
sollen often reports advice or instructions from a doctor or another person.
With sollen, the infinitive still stays at the end.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Wartet Sie bitte hier!
review_tasks.why: The polite command uses the infinitive Warten followed by Sie.

review_tasks.prompt: Explain this pattern aloud. Then write a new sentence using it:
review_tasks.question: verb (infinitive) + Sie + ... + bitte
review_tasks.why: Compare your verb position, case endings and meaning to the model.

review_tasks.model: Example starting point: Ich soll morgen zum Arzt gehen.

lessons.title: Informal commands and object pronouns
lessons.goal: Give du/ihr instructions and replace objects with pronouns.
lessons.formula: du imperative: Komm!; ihr imperative: Kommt!
explanations: The informal du imperative often uses the verb stem, while ihr uses the familiar ihr verb form without ihr.
Accusative personal pronouns include mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch and sie/Sie.

examples.de: Ich sehe den Hund. Ich sehe ihn.
examples.en: I see the dog. I see it.

trap.why: The du subject is normally omitted in the imperative.

lessons.challenge: Make two requests to a friend and two to a group, then replace three objects with pronouns.
deep_notes: Imperatives in du and ihr use different verb forms; the subject is omitted.
Objects are replaced by pronouns that match the object's grammatical gender and case.
mich/dich/ihn answer Wen?; mir/dir/ihm answer Wem? (dative).
Some verbs have irregular du commands, e.g. Lies! or Nimm!

lessons.title: Past participles without ge-
lessons.goal: Recognize common inseparable-prefix participles and the prefix un-.
explanations: Verbs beginning be-, ver- or er- form participles without ge-, e.g. bezahlt, verstanden, erzählt.
Adjectives with un- often express the opposite: möglich/unmöglich, pünktlich/unpünktlich.

trap.why: An er- verb does not take extra ge- in the participle.

lessons.challenge: Explain a past problem in four sentences using two inseparable-prefix verbs.
deep_notes: Prefixes be-, ver- and er- are typically inseparable: their participles omit ge-.
A typical regular past participle ends -t even without ge-: bezahlt.
Un- can make an adjective's opposite, but not all adjectives allow it.
Watch for e.g. bekommen as a verb; its past form is bekommen, not gebekommen.

quiz.explanation: be- verbs usually take no extra ge-.
er- verbs form participles without ge-.
ver- verbs do not use ge-.
un- can form the opposite adjective.

review_tasks.why: An er- verb does not take extra ge- in the participle.

lessons.title: müssen, dürfen, man and modal contrast
lessons.goal: Distinguish necessity, permission and prohibition.
explanations: müssen means must or have to. dürfen means may or be allowed. nicht dürfen means prohibited; nicht müssen means not necessary.
man is an impersonal subject (one/people in general), and takes third-person singular verbs.

examples.en: You don't have to come today.

trap.why: Prohibition requires nicht dürfen, not nicht müssen.

lessons.challenge: Describe three rules and three permissions at work, school or in your building.
deep_notes: müssen + nicht expresses no obligation: you may, but you don't have to.
dürfen + nicht means forbidden; this is stronger than a lack of obligation.
man is grammatically third-person singular: man darf, man muss.
Use wollen for intention, können for ability, dürfen for permission, sollen for advice.

review_tasks.prompt: Spot and repair the grammar mistake:
review_tasks.question: Du musst hier nicht rauchen (forbidden).
review_tasks.why: Prohibition requires nicht dürfen, not nicht müssen.

lessons.title: Comparisons and demonstratives
lessons.goal: Compare things with als/wie and choose welche/diese forms.
explanations: Comparative adjectives often add -er; equal comparisons use so ... wie, unequal comparisons use comparative + als.
welch- asks which; dies- means this/these. Their endings depend on the noun and its case.

examples.de: Mein Zimmer ist heller als deins.
examples.en: My room is brighter than yours.

examples.de: Dieses Kleid ist genauso teuer wie das andere.
examples.en: This dress is just as expensive as the other.

trap.why: Buch is neuter; use dieses in nominative.

lessons.challenge: Compare two apartments or products with four different adjectives.
deep_notes: The comparison adjective follows its own patterns: groß -> größer; gut -> besser.
Use als with a difference and wie with equal degree: so groß wie.
Superlatives with am often end -sten: am schnellsten.
welch- asks for a choice and dies- points out a particular item; endings matter.

lessons.title: Connectors and two-way prepositions
lessons.goal: Link ideas and distinguish location from direction.
explanations: und, aber, oder and denn join main clauses without moving the finite verb to the end.
Two-way prepositions such as in/auf/an use dative for location (wo?) and accusative for destination (wohin?).

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin müde.
examples.en: I'm staying home because I'm tired.

examples.de: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The book is lying on the table.

examples.de: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
examples.en: I put the book on the table.

trap.wrong: Ich gehe in der Küche hinein.
trap.why: For motion into a location, use accusative.

lessons.challenge: Explain where three things are and where you move them; connect two thoughts with denn.
deep_notes: Connectors und, aber, oder, denn join full main clauses without changing verb-second order.
For place prepositions ask Wo? (location) or Wohin? (movement to a place).
auf dem Tisch describes position; auf den Tisch describes placement.
Some verbs pair with physical states: liegen/legen and stehen/stellen.

lessons.title: Dates, ordinal numbers and würde
lessons.goal: Say dates and express wishes politely.
lessons.formula: am + ordinal ending; würde + gern + infinitive
explanations: Ordinal numbers name an order or a calendar date: der erste Mai; am ersten Mai.
würde + infinitive expresses polite or hypothetical wishes: Ich würde gern ... . It is an extension useful at the end of A1.

examples.en: Today is the fourth of April.

examples.de: Mein Termin ist am siebten Juni.
examples.en: My appointment is on June seventh.
I would like to travel more.

trap.wrong: Ich habe am drei Mai Geburtstag.
trap.correct: Ich habe am dritten Mai Geburtstag.
trap.why: After am, use the dative ordinal ending -en.

lessons.challenge: Tell three important dates and write a wish list with würde gern.
deep_notes: Ordinal numbers indicate rank or dates, not basic quantities.
With an unintroduced calendar date use der erste Mai; after am use am ersten Mai.
würde + infinitive is a polite or hypothetical wish rather than ordinary future.
The user should recognize months, numbers and their spoken forms as one package.
